Plain linked-list queue with head_mutex + tail_mutex fails: on an empty queue push() sets both head and tail; with one item push() writes tail->next and try_pop() reads head->next (same node). try_pop can't 'check for one item first' because that needs tail, i.e. tail_mutex on every call -> same mutex as push, no gain. Dummy node keeps head and tail on different nodes; cost: data stored by pointer (extra indirection).

Which user code runs while the stack's lock is held (push: move ctor + allocation; pop(): allocation + move ctor; pop(T&): move ASSIGNMENT; copy ctor: element copies under other.m), the two deadlocks it enables (lock-order inversion with a user mutex; re-entering the same stack), and why the book leaves it to the user.

Why a hash table allows a lock per bucket and why get_bucket() takes no lock: with a fixed number of buckets, a key's bucket depends only on the key and the hash function, so finding it touches nothing shared that ever changes. Resizing / rehashing would break this. Tree: every op passes the root; sorted array: can't know where a value is in advance, so one lock for the whole array.

get_map() (Listing 6.12) must hold every bucket's lock at once to copy a consistent state; reading buckets one at a time can show a later insert while missing an earlier one. It's the only op taking more than one bucket lock, and it takes them in a fixed order (increasing bucket index), so no deadlock.

Hand-over-hand locking (6.13): lock the next node before unlocking the current one, always starting from head and moving one way, so all threads take node locks in the same order (no deadlock) and can't pass each other. remove_if may destroy the unlinked node after unlocking its mutex because it still holds the previous node's lock, so no thread can reach the dead node. Unlocking current before locking next lets a remover delete the next node under you (use-after-free).

Why the 6.3.2 list has no STL iterators and what for_each costs: an iterator would have to hold a lock on part of the list, and its lifetime is outside the container's control. for_each calls user code while holding the node lock (breaks ch3's 'don't call user-supplied code while holding a lock') and passes it a reference to each item. Alternative: pass a copy of each item, which is expensive for large items. The book leaves deadlock/race avoidance to the user's functions; fine for the lookup table, whose predicates only compare keys.

Listing 7.6: the set-and-recheck loop compares head with a pointer whose object may already be deleted; using a pointer's value after delete is technically UB with default new/delete, so the implementation must permit it or use a custom allocator. compare_exchange_strong because there's work inside the loop (a spurious weak failure would reset the hazard pointer unnecessarily). Clear the hazard pointer right after the successful CAS: the node is now off the stack and only this thread can reach it. Nodes still hazardous after delete_nodes_with_no_hazards() stay on the list for the next pop().

Naive hazard pointers: every pop() scans max_hazard_pointers atomics for its node and again for each pending node (atomics often ~100x slower than plain ops). Improvement 1: only reclaim when the list has 2*max_hazard_pointers nodes -> at least max reclaimed, then >= max pops before the next attempt: about 2 nodes checked per pop, 1 reclaimed (max+1 barely helps: you'd try nearly every pop and reclaim ~1). Still needs an atomic count and the list is still contended. Improvement 2: per-thread (thread_local) reclaim lists: no atomics for count or list, but up to max*max nodes allocated; an exiting thread's leftovers go to a global list, picked up by the next reclaiming thread.

Why pop() stores the hazard pointer then re-reads head until equal: between reading head and publishing the hazard pointer no other thread knows this node is being accessed, so it could be popped, checked (no hazards) and deleted, and the dereference would be use-after-free. If head still equals the value after the hazard pointer is set, the node was still on the stack after the hazard pointer became visible, so anyone removing it later will see it. head unchanged is enough because a node can only be deleted after it's been removed from head. After a failed CAS reloads old_head, the hazard pointer still names the OLD node, so the new one must be re-protected before dereferencing.

Listing 7.7: a thread claims a hazard-pointer slot by CAS on the slot's owner id (empty id -> this thread's id) on first use, cached in a thread_local hp_owner; throws if no slot is free. At thread exit the destructor clears the pointer FIRST, then resets the id; resetting the id first lets another thread claim the slot and set its hazard pointer, which the late pointer-clear then wipes out. outstanding_hazard_pointers_for() scans every slot without checking owners (unowned slots hold nullptr).

Listing 7.11: pop() increments the external count in head BEFORE dereferencing ptr; otherwise another thread could pop and free the node between the load and the access (dangling pointer). increase_head_count() does a compare/exchange on the whole counted_node_ptr, so the increment only lands if head still holds the same pointer -- the count and the pointer change together, which a separately stored counter couldn't guarantee.

7.2 intro/7.2.1: only std::atomic_flag is guaranteed not to use locks; on some platforms 'lock-free' code uses locks inside the library, and a simple lock-based structure may be better -- identify requirements and profile first. Listing 7.3 is lock-free but not wait-free: push/pop CAS loops can in theory retry forever if the exchange keeps failing.

Lock-free pop() can't use pop(T&) for exception safety: the value may only be copied once this thread's CAS has removed the node, so a throwing copy loses it anyway. Return std::shared_ptr<T> (returning it can't throw), with the T allocated in push() (a node is allocated there anyway; allocating in pop() could throw after removal). Listing 7.4 swaps the data out so a pending node doesn't keep the T alive.

delete_nodes_with_no_hazards() must claim the whole list with exchange(nullptr) first. Walking the shared list instead: two threads can delete the same entry (double delete, UB); entries are deleted while still linked, so the shared head / other entries point at freed memory, and a concurrent add_to_reclaim_list() links its node to a freed entry -> later walks read freed memory. exchange makes this thread the only one reclaiming that set; others may still add new entries or reclaim them.

try_reclaim() (Listing 7.5): after seeing threads_in_pop == 1, claim the pending list and do the 'count reached zero?' test BEFORE deleting old_head, because deleting is slow: the longer the gap between first seeing 1 and claiming/rechecking, the more likely another thread has entered pop() and the count is no longer 1, so the pending nodes can't be reclaimed. (Deleting old_head itself is safe in that branch: it was popped while this thread was alone.)

7.2.4: std::shared_ptr's atomic operations aren't guaranteed lock-free because making them lock-free would add overhead to every use of the class; check with std::atomic_is_lock_free(&sp) -- if true, Listing 7.9 (shared_ptr links) makes the reclamation problem go away. counted_node_ptr {int; node*} is a plain struct, so std::atomic<> accepts it; it's lock-free only where double-word compare-and-swap exists; otherwise std::atomic<> uses a mutex inside, making the 'lock-free' stack lock-based, and the book suggests the shared_ptr version instead. push() sets external_count = 1 because the only external reference is head itself.

Listing 7.11: the winner adds (external_count - 2) to internal_count: -1 because the node is no longer in the list (head's reference), -1 because this thread is done with it. It deletes if fetch_add returned -(external-2), i.e. the sum hit zero. A loser (its CAS on head failed) does internal_count.fetch_sub(1) on the node it was trying to pop (ptr, not the refreshed old_head) and deletes if that returned 1. Whichever of them brings the total to zero deletes, so exactly one thread deletes, after everyone is done.

Why try_reclaim() rechecks threads_in_pop after claiming the pending list (Figure 7.1): between A's 'count == 1' test and its exchange, B enters pop() and reads head = Y; C pops Y, sees count > 1 and chains Y onto to_be_deleted; A's exchange claims Y. If A deleted without rechecking, B's CAS would read Y->next after free. Recheck (decrement to zero) means no one in pop() can hold a pointer into the claimed list; otherwise chain it back.

Listing 7.8: reclaim_later is a template and data_to_reclaim stores void* plus a std::function deleter pointing at do_delete<T>, because hazard pointers are general-purpose (any pointer type, stored as void*) but delete needs the real type to run T's destructor. The deleter runs in ~data_to_reclaim, called only once no hazard pointer references the data.

Reduction step (for_each: a no-op); the book's two ways to parallelize it (accumulate calls itself recursively; workers do reduction steps as each finishes); std::async lets the library choose new thread vs synchronous; a thread per recursion: too many threads slow it down, and you can run out; Listing 8.1's costs: complexity, and contention on the one shared stack; it is a specialized thread pool
hardware_concurrency() may return 0; unsigned hardware_concurrency()-1 then wraps to UINT_MAX, so Listing 8.1 starts a thread per chunk; fall back to a fixed count
Listing 8.1: a thread waiting for its lower chunk sorts chunks off the stack; a plain get() hangs with zero workers, or when every thread is waiting on chunks still on the stack

Wrong concerns = too much communication; remedies: all of it about one issue -> make it one thread's job; two threads chatting mostly to each other -> combine them. A pipeline fits when the input isn't all known at the start, or each step is time consuming. It makes output regular; it does not lower first-item latency, and total time gets longer
Worker threads run do_sort too, so Listing 8.1's threads.size() check and push_back race (a data race on the vector); the check-and-start needs a lock (or start every worker up front)

Raise P: shrink the serial sections or the time threads wait, or give more data so the parallel sections stay primed; the two aspects of scalability: less time per action vs more data per unit time; pick which matters before dividing work
Listing 8.5 is exception safe because destroying a std::async future without waiting makes its destructor wait for the task (no dangling thread); the async task's exception comes back through get()

Exception safety is correctness (broken invariants, races, terminate) while code that doesn't scale still works; Listing 8.5 gets its thread use from the library, which avoids an overwhelming number of threads, and some async calls run synchronously in get(), so NOT one new thread per call
Listing 8.4 reads the futures before joining because get() blocks until that task is done; Listing 8.2's results vector needed the join first

Listing 8.6: Start while a task runs move-assigns onto a joinable std::thread -> std::terminate; task_complete handled after Stop already joined -> join() on a non-joinable thread throws std::system_error; Stop's join() blocks the GUI thread until the current step ends

Listing 8.2 dies two ways: an exception escaping a spawned thread's function, and a joinable std::thread destroyed during unwinding (a later thread constructor or the caller's own block throws); packaged_task + future fixes the first, join_threads the second

Barrier: read generation before taking a seat; the last arrival refills spaces from count, then bumps generation; waiters spin on generation, not spaces; done_waiting() must decrement spaces as well as count, or the current round never completes

parallel_find (8.9) joins every thread before checking done_flag: if nothing matched, no one sets the promise and get() would block for ever; the flag only means something once every searcher has finished

Listing 8.11: each block waits on the previous block's last value (future), updates its own last element first and passes it on (promise), then updates the rest; exceptions travel down the promise chain to the caller's block. Tasks wait on each other mid-run, so it can't be written with std::async
packaged_task is move-only and std::function needs copyable callables, so the waitable pool queues a type-erased, move-only function_wrapper (virtual call through a unique_ptr)

Thread-local queues cut contention on the shared queue, but unbalance the load (Quicksort: nearly everything lands on one worker's queue); work stealing fixes it: the pool owns every queue, the owner pushes and pops at the front (LIFO), and thieves take from the back
Thread pool members: done flag and queue(s) first, then the threads vector, then join_threads; members are destroyed in reverse, so the joiner joins every worker while the queue still exists
Tasks that wait for other tasks on a fixed-size pool must run pending tasks while waiting (run_pending_task loop); a plain get() can leave every worker blocked on work nobody is free to run
